body_html:
I think, inheriting code from other developers, can be a struggle. There, I said it!
That’s because not two developers think alike — everyone has his or hers way of doing things.

Having said that, here’s my personal take on how to tackle code-share between (front-end-) developers:

Think in modules.

No matter what you create on a site, being it an article, an accordion-, spot- or a video-block, think of it as an individual module, with it’s own version number and “module-like” structure:

<!-- Accordion Block. Version 1.2.5 -->
<section class="accordion">
	<h2 class="accordion-header">
		Accordion header
	</h2>
	
	<div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/Question">
		<input type="radio" class="state" id="id1" name="grp_accordion" />
		<label for="id1" class="accordion-label" itemprop="text" accesskey="1">
			<span class="accordion-label-inner">Question 1</span>
		</label>
		<div class="accordion-panel" itemprop="suggestedAnswer acceptedAnswer" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/Answer">
			<div class="accordion-panel-text" itemprop="text">
				Text
			</div>
		</div>
	</div>

	<div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/Question">
		<input type="radio" class="state" id="id2" name="grp_accordion" />
		<label for="id2" class="accordion-label" itemprop="text" accesskey="2">
			<span class="accordion-label-inner">Question 2</span>
		</label>
		<div class="accordion-panel" itemprop="suggestedAnswer acceptedAnswer" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/Answer">
			<div class="accordion-panel-text" itemprop="text">
				Text
			</div>
		</div>
	</div>
</section>

If any of the markup change, change the version-number, so you know which existing implementations of the module would have to be updated as well.

Use a BEM-like structure for the markup — there are various versions, I prefer the simple version, using hyphens for elements.

Assign classes to everything! Even though it may be cumbersome to add the class accordion-header to the h2-element, because you want all h2-elements on your site to be the same, do it anyway. It will save you a lot of headaches in the future (when the marketing-department want all h2’s in the accordion-block to be blue, and all h2’s in the video-block to be red!)!

Make sure that the HTML is rock-solid and validates: both the HTML itself, but also the structured markup.

Next, create a SASS mixin with the same (BEM-) structure as the HTML:

@mixin accordion($theme: $accordion) {
  &-header {
    ...
  } 
  &-label {
    ...
  }

Use sassDOC to document the mixin, provide version-number, examples etc:

/// Accordion-module, can either toggle (by using checkboxes in the HTML) or collapse (by using radio-buttons)
/// - Version 1.2.5
/// - Date last edited: 2016-04-07
/// @name accordion
/// @group blocks
/// @author Mads Stoumann
/// @param {String} $theme [$accordion]- The theme-map to use
/// @output class-module
/// @link http://www.stoumann.dk/blocks/accordion.html Demo
/// @example scss
///   .accordion ( @include accordion(); )

Theme-maps

Did you notice the default $theme-parameter in the mixin? In this case, it expects a theme-map called $accordion.

A theme-object could look like this:

$accordion: (
	"border-color": #aaa,
	"font-map": 0,
	"label-background": linear-gradient(to bottom, #ddd, #eee),
	"label-color": #333,
	"label-font-size": 1.125em,
	"padding": 1em,
	"panel-max-height": 50em,
	"text-background": "#fff",
	"text-color": "#222",
	"toggle-contract": "\2212",
	"toggle-expand": "\002B",
	"toggle-font-family": "Roboto, sans-serif",
	"toggle-font-size": 2em,
	"toggle-position": right
);

To access one of the values from the theme-map, use the map-get function:

  border: 1px solid map-get($theme, "border-color");
  background: map-get($theme, "label-background");

Create as many key/value-pairs as necessary for the theme-map, and finally, create a class that calls the mixin:

.accordion { @include accordion(); }

You can then experiment with an alternate theme-map, let’s call it $custom-accordion, and call it like this:

.accordion { @include accordion($custom-accordion); }

And if you want both versions on your site:

.accordion { 
  @include accordion();
  .custom-accordion & { @include accordion($custom-accordion); }
}

In the HTML, prefix or suffix the first selector with the custom class:

<section class="accordion custom-accordion"> ...

Font-maps

To create even more flexible modules, use them with a font-map.

It’s basically which root font-size to use per media query.

If your breakpoints look like this:

/// @name breakpoints
/// @group config
$breakpoints: (
	"phone"			: 0,
	"phablet"		: 640px,
	"tablet"		: 768px,
	"desktop"		: 1024px,
	"desktop-large"	: 1280px,
	"desktop-xlarge": 1600px
) !default;

— Your default font-map might look like this:

/// @name fontrootsizes
/// @group config
$fontrootsizes: (
	"phone"			: 13px,
	"phablet"		: 14px,
	"tablet"		: 15px,
	"desktop"		: 16px,
	"desktop-large"	: 17px,
	"desktop-xlarge": 18px
) !default;

— so in “phone”-mode, in this case, the root font-size will be 13px.

Now, if you set your font-sizes in em within the mixin, let’s say the accordion-header:

...
&-header { font-size: 2em; }
...

— The size will dynamically resize or shrink based on the root-sizes. In “phone-mode” it will be 26px, in “tablet-mode” it will be 30px.

Finally …

Now, when sending the code to other developers — hopefully — all they have to work on will be theme-maps!

But even if they do change the HTML or the associated mixin, it will be with a different version-number — but hopefully backwards-compatible with existing implementations.

I personally think, that if you think in modules, the code you create will be more re-usable and easier to read, because it forces you to approach the HTML and (S)CSS in a different way.

Happy coding!
